blocks.prompt: The Nose That Knows
blocks.text: You see the world. Your dog smells it. A dog has hundreds of millions of tiny smell catchers inside its nose. You have about six million. That is why a dog can find a lost sock under the couch, or one crumb of cheese in the grass. A dog's nose is wet because wet skin grabs smells out of the air. When your dog sniffs fast, it is pulling new air over those smell catchers again and again. A dog can smell who walked down your street this morning. It can smell them even after they have gone home.

blocks.prompt: How a Dog's Nose Really Works
blocks.text: When you breathe in, one stream of air goes to your lungs, and whatever smells ride along get noticed on the way. A dog's nose does something smarter. Inside each nostril, the air splits into two paths. Most of it goes down to the lungs. A small stream peels off into a maze of curled bone covered in smell catchers, and that air stays there to be studied. Then look at the slits on the sides of a dog's nose. When a dog breathes out, the used air shoots out sideways instead of straight ahead. That way it does not blow the scent away. It actually swirls fresh air toward the nostrils for the next sniff. A dog also sniffs with each nostril a little separately, so it can tell which side a smell came from. Best of all, a dog can smell how old a scent is. A footprint from ten minutes ago smells stronger than one from an hour ago. Follow the trail toward the stronger prints and you are walking the way the person walked. Your dog is not just smelling the yard. It is smelling this morning.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.

answers: it splits into two paths, one to the lungs and one to the smell catchers
the used air does not blow the scent away, and it swirls fresh air in
a fresher footprint smells stronger, so it follows the stronger prints
(inference: two nostrils let it tell which side a smell came from)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Puppies follow pointing at eight weeks
Wolves mostly cannot do it

Shared gaze raises oxytocin in both

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Watches Your Hands
blocks.text: Point at something across the room and your dog will look where you are pointing. That sounds like nothing. It is not nothing. Chimpanzees are our closest relatives, and they are terrible at it. Wolves raised by people from birth mostly fail too. Puppies do it at eight weeks old, before anyone has trained them to. Researchers set up a simple test. Food is hidden under one of two cups. A person points at the correct cup. Does the animal understand that the point is a message meant for it? Dogs do. They understand that a human hand is trying to tell them something, and they trust it. There is a second test that is stranger. Give an animal a puzzle box with food inside, then rig the box so it cannot be opened. A wolf keeps working at the box until it gives up. A dog works at the box for a while, then stops and turns around and looks at the nearest human face. It asks for help. Nobody taught it that either. Scientists also found that when a dog and its owner look into each other's eyes, both of their brains release oxytocin, the same chemical that rises between a parent and a baby. The dog stares. The human feels warm. The human feeds the dog. The loop is quiet, and it works. Dogs did not just move into our houses. They learned to read us.

blocks.prompt: The Wolf That Sat Down
blocks.text: Somewhere between fifteen thousand and forty thousand years ago, a wolf did something no wolf had done before. It sat down near a human camp and did not run. Nobody knows exactly how it happened, and the leading explanation gives humans very little credit. It is called self-domestication. Human camps produced garbage: bones, scraps, the parts of animals nobody wanted. Garbage is food. But approaching a camp full of people takes nerve. A wolf that panicked at every voice starved at the edge of the firelight. A wolf that could tolerate humans ate well, survived winter, and had pups that could also tolerate humans. Generation after generation, the calmest wolves at the dump out-ate the nervous ones. People did not tame wolves. Tameness paid, and the wolves selected themselves. Something odd came with the tameness. In 1959, a Russian scientist named Dmitry Belyaev began breeding silver foxes on one rule only: he kept the foxes that were least afraid of a human hand and bred those. He selected for nothing else. No ear shape, no coat pattern, no tail. Within a few dozen generations his foxes had floppy ears, curly tails, patches of white fur, shorter snouts, and a habit of whining for attention. He had bred for a feeling and accidentally grown a dog. Biologists have a name for that bundle of changes: domestication syndrome. One popular explanation points to a group of cells in the developing embryo called neural crest cells. They help build the adrenal glands, which drive fear, and they also help build ear cartilage, snouts, and pigment. Turn down the fear system a little and you may quietly turn down all the rest as well. That idea is still argued over. The pattern itself is not. One last thing worth knowing. The dog is ancient, but breeds are not. The pug, the dachshund, the golden retriever and most of the rest were shaped in the last two hundred years or so, largely by Victorian hobbyists competing at dog shows. Your dog's mind is tens of thousands of years old. Its face is Victorian.

meta.templateLabel: The Dog That Learned to Read Us

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Levator anguli oculi medialis
The eyebrow muscle wolves lack
Coded AU101 in the dog facial system
Shelter dogs using it are rehomed faster
Domestication: 15,000 to 40,000 years ago

blocks.prompt: The Muscle That Wolves Do Not Have
blocks.text: In 2019, a team of anatomists did something that sounds grim and turned out to be revealing. They dissected the faces of dogs and the faces of gray wolves, muscle by muscle, and compared them. The two animals are close enough that they can still interbreed, and their faces were nearly identical. Nearly. Above the inner corner of each dog's eye sat a small muscle called the levator anguli oculi medialis. In the wolves, it was almost absent: a thin strand of tissue, or nothing at all. That muscle has one job. It lifts the inner eyebrow. It is the muscle behind the expression every dog owner knows, the one where the head stays down and the eyebrows go up and the eyes suddenly look enormous and sad. Researchers call it AU101. Everyone else calls it puppy dog eyes. Here is why a single muscle is worth a scientific paper. That expression makes a dog's eye look bigger and its face look more like a baby's, and it closely resembles the face a human makes when we are sad. Humans respond to it without deciding to. In shelter studies, dogs that produced the expression more often were rehomed faster. Not the friendliest dogs. Not the healthiest. The ones with the better eyebrows. Follow that logic to the end. Wolves became dogs over tens of thousands of years of living beside people. Across those millennia, the dogs that got fed were the dogs that humans found hard to ignore. A dog that could reach into a human's emotional wiring got scraps, shelter, a place by the fire, and pups. Over enough generations, that pressure did not just change dog behavior. It grew new anatomy. Human feelings became a selection pressure strong enough to build a muscle. Notice who is being manipulated in this story. We tend to tell domestication as something people did to animals: we captured wolves, we tamed them, we bred them into shape. The muscle complicates that. It is evidence of animals evolving to work on us, targeting a weakness we cannot switch off, because you cannot decide not to find a puppy's face moving. We did not consent to any of it. We just kept feeding whichever ones looked at us right. None of this means your dog is lying to you. A muscle is not a plan. The dog making the face is not calculating; it inherited a face that works on humans, exactly as a bird inherits a wing it never designed. Other research complicates the picture in a useful way: dogs make more expressions when a human is looking at them than when a human's back is turned, whether or not food is present, which suggests the face is aimed at attention rather than at snacks. What the muscle really shows is that the relationship went both ways. Dogs did not simply move in with us. They changed shape around us, down to the fibers above their eyes, and in return they rearranged us too. We built a species that reads our faces, and then we made room for it in our beds. Two animals, thirty thousand years, one long conversation held mostly without words.
